new_articles.title: Divergent associations of exercise-intensity-related lactate responses with Stroop interference and working memory accuracy
new_articles.abstract: Acute aerobic exercise modulates cognition and prefrontal haemodynamics, but physiological markers associated with heterogeneous responses to exercise intensities remain unclear. This randomised crossover study examined whether lactate and heart rate variability (HRV), indexing metabolic and autonomic recovery, were associated with executive function and haemodynamic outcomes following acute moderate-intensity continuous training (MICT) and high-intensity interval training (HIIT). Fifty-five young adults (56% male) completed both conditions. Capillary lactate, wrist-derived HRV, 2-back and Stroop performance, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS)-derived task-evoked prefrontal haemodynamics were assessed pre- and post-exercise. Linear mixed models showed pre-to-post improvement in 2-back reaction-time (RT) and accuracy, Stroop incongruent and interference RT, irrespective of condition. HIIT elicited greater increases in lactate. Exploratory time-moderated mediation showed HIIT relative to MICT was indirectly associated through lactate with higher Stroop interference accuracy (β = 0.10, 95%CI = 0.03, 0.18) and lower 2-back accuracy (β = −0.08, 95%CI= −0.16, −0.002). Lactate was indirectly associated with congruent Stroop Δ[HbO] (β = 0.14, 95%CI = 0.03, 0.25), without corresponding behavioural change. HRV showed no indirect associations. These findings suggest that lactate-related associations may vary between executive function outcomes rather than reflect a uniform cognitive benefit. Given the exploratory nature of these analyses and the modest precision of indirect estimates, replication is warranted.

new_articles.title: Beyond performance scores: directed functional connectivity as a brain-based biomarker for tracking motor skill learning and retention
new_articles.abstract: Surgical motor skill acquisition requires prolonged training and durable retention, yet standard behavioral metrics capture performance changes without revealing the neural mechanisms of learning. Here, we validate directed functional connectivity (dFC)—computed from electroencephalography across five cortical regions using nonlinear Granger causality—as a brain-based biomarker for tracking motor learning and retention. Twenty-five trainees completed a 15-day laparoscopic suturing program followed by six-week retention testing; an untrained control group (n = 27) and 15 expert surgeons served as behavioral and autonomous-stage references. dFC was evaluated using subtask-level decomposition, change-point detection, and a one-dimensional convolutional neural network benchmarked against the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery (FLS) score. dFC classified pre- versus post-training trials with 94.4% accuracy, outperforming the FLS-based classifier (84.5%), while matching FLS on pre- versus retention discrimination (87.5% vs. 88.5%). Notably, dFC identified the cognitive-to-associative transition one day later (day 6) than behavioral metrics (day 5), consistent with sleep-dependent neural consolidation. Neither measure changed further from post-training to retention, and controls exhibited no adaptation. Individual-level dFC measures tracked behavioral cumulative sum (CUSUM) trajectories. Overall, dFC provides a subtask-level, longitudinally stable biomarker of neural adaptation that complements behavioral metrics and holds potential for brain-informed surgical training.
